publicSources.title: [Hero Run] 535B-A23B on 18T tokens
publicSources.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

publicSources.title: [grug] Ragged EP train step hangs silently on one rack at d6144 hero scale
publicSources.body:
The ragged all-to-all EP backend hangs at the d6144 hero scale (11 racks, 704 GPUs) within the first hundred steps, on both attempts of the 2026-09-02 deployment. The train step never completes on one rack, the other ten spin in the next AllReduce, and levanter's progress watchdog kills the gang 15 minutes later (`No progress after train_step_started for 909.8 seconds (timeout 900.0); terminating with exit code 124`). No rank logs an error: nothing from NCCL, XLA, CUDA (no Xid), the allocator, or Kubernetes. The hero was rolled back to `04751985c7` (pooled-wave backend), which resumed cleanly from the same checkpoint.

Deployment: main `8e48cdb3ca`, run `hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k` resuming `hero-12d8b6f0-dee637` from its `step-54000` permanent checkpoint (#8868), `HERO_WATCH_INTERVAL = 10`, `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel=true --xla_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers_for_collectives=raggedalltoall`, jax 0.11.1, NCCL 2.30.7. Coordinator `/marin/hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k-coord-aade2815`; both attempts ran on the same 176 nodes.

- Attempt 0: steps 54001–54070 completed normally (loss tracks the pooled-wave run step for step at −0.006 nats, drops 3.4e-2 → <1e-4, MFU 20.5 → 23.4%, peak HBM 103.6 GiB). Step 54071 started at 00:23:30Z and never finished; killed 00:38:46Z.
- Attempt 1: restored the same checkpoint, completed step 54000 at 00:45:38Z (loss 1.2364, identical to attempt 0), then hung on step 54001; killed ~01:01Z.

Both hangs are on the first plain train step after a `diagnostic_watch_step` step (54070 → 54071 after seven clean alternations; 54000 → 54001 on the first). The plain and watch steps are two XLA executables that share the NCCL symmetric-memory arena for the ragged all-to-all: each registers its own window at the arena base (`AcquireSymmetricMemory`, `CollectiveMemoryCache`), and equal footprints coexist. #8861 is the same design failing the other way: an executable with a *different* footprint (the capacity-limited eval) makes the next train step fail with `ncclGroupEnd() failed: invalid argument`. Here the footprints are equal and the failure is a silent hang instead of an error, so #8859 (dropless eval only) removes the crash but not this.

Evidence that the hang sits on one rack's EP domain rather than a node fault:

- NCCL RAS (periodic `STATUS` from process 0, `telemetry_v1.levanter`): six minutes into each hang, 64 cross-rack communicators show an AllReduce operation-count skew of exactly 3 (attempt 0: min 10509 / max 10512 at 00:29:43Z; attempt 1: 190 / 193 at 00:52:30Z) and the 704-rank communicator a skew of 2. Before the hangs every communicator was in sync. One member per cross-rack communicator behind by the same count is one whole rack that never entered the step's trailing AllReduces.
- Iris per-task CPU (`iris.task`): exactly 16 of 176 tasks ran at ~4.0 cores while the other 160 ran at ~8.0 during each hang, i.e. one rack in a different wait state from the ranks busy-polling in AllReduce. Attempt 0: tasks 128–143 (zone 129, nodes `s38vxs64 s45sxs64 s51vxs64 s5xvxs64 s69vxs64 s7htxs64 s7qvxs64 s8ktxs64 s8mtxs64 s8yvxs64 s9jvxs64 s9lrxs64 scspxs64 scssxs64 sd8sxs64 shmsxs64`). Attempt 1: tasks 64–79, a different rack on the same node set.
- py-spy thread dumps (`iris process profile threads`) of tasks 0, 83, and 140 during attempt 0: every rank's main thread inside `train_step` (`train.py:1176`), no Python-side wait; the hang is below XLA's dispatch.
- No node conditions or events on either rack; the cluster's six `HPCVerification=Fail` nodes are elsewhere.

The stall-triggered verbose RAS capture (`trigger = stall`) published nothing in either attempt, so the rank-level view that would name the stuck ranks and the pending collective is missing; the periodic sample is all we have. Neither a 200-step 1-rack smoke restoring the same checkpoint (20 watch/plain alternations) nor the 11,420-step d768 rung reproduced it, so the failure needs more than one rack, i.e. more than one EP domain sharing the job.

Side observations from the same deployment: a cold compile at this shape took 22.9 min for the watch executable plus 6.6 min for the plain one; the data loader's second 64-item prefetch took 920 s (overlapped by compile) where the pooled-wave hero's restarts took under 100 s.

Done when: the ragged backend runs at 11 racks through at least several hundred steps with watch steps enabled without a hang, or the hang is reproduced at smaller multi-rack scale with a GPU-side stack (CUDA core dump / `cuda-gdb` on a stuck rank) that names the kernel or collective.

Related: #8861 (symmetric-window overlap between executables), #8859, #8868, #8506 (hero status log). Side-by-side trial report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/ep_change:-hero-ragged-a2a-swap,-200-step-trial--VmlldzoxNzg1ODIzMA==

publicSources.title: [grug] Diagnose recurring hero timestamp gaps outside the step timer
publicSources.body:
Diagnose the recurring excess of time between W&B history rows over `throughput/duration` on the 535B-A23B hero run. The pattern occurs before and after disabling QuACK programmatic dependent launch (PDL) in #9183. Its cause and end-to-end throughput cost are unresolved.

A September 16 read of consecutive W&B history rows found:

| Measurement | [Control, PDL enabled](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-mix-996f4891-step108k) | [Trial, PDL disabled](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-nopdl-step108k) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| History steps | 108000–108981 | 108778–112667 |
| Eligible adjacent intervals | 976 | 3,886 |
| Intervals with excess >1.2 s | 40.37% | 40.84% |
| Median timestamp interval, quiet / slow | 16.963 / 18.369 s | 16.661 / 18.172 s |
| Median training duration, quiet / slow | 16.704 / 16.717 s | 16.387 / 16.417 s |
| Median excess, quiet / slow | 0.236 / 1.584 s | 0.240 / 1.645 s |

Reproduce the measurement:

1. Fetch unsampled history for the linked runs over the listed step ranges, including `_step`, `_timestamp`, `throughput/duration`, `throughput/hook_time`, and `throughput/loading_time`.
2. For adjacent rows whose `_step` values differ by exactly one, compute `interval = timestamp[i] - timestamp[i-1]` and `excess = interval - duration[i]`. Retain `0 < interval < 60` seconds and `duration[i] < 40` seconds to exclude startup and large interruptions.
3. Classify quiet intervals as `excess < 0.8` seconds and slow intervals as `excess > 1.2` seconds. Compute each column's median independently; median excess need not equal the difference of medians.
4. To locate sustained stretches, take a trailing 12-interval median of excess and retain runs above 1.2 seconds lasting more than 20 intervals. The start-to-start spacing on the trial grows from roughly 67–73 toward 75–83 minutes after startup; control stretches recur roughly 32–42 minutes apart excluding the 116-minute spacing that spans its interruption. The period is not fixed at 80 minutes.

In both groups and both runs, median `throughput/hook_time` is about 4.6 ms and `throughput/loading_time` about 25 microseconds. These recorded timers do not explain the roughly 1.6-second excess in slow intervals.

The [trial build’s training loop](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8f6f33bebe681ed12ff88a6ed14121990bf2cec3/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L1160) stops the step timer before callbacks, later metric materialization, and checkpoint handling; the next batch load also falls outside it. [Background tracking](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8f6f33bebe681ed12ff88a6ed14121990bf2cec3/lib/levanter/src/levanter/tracker/background.py#L12) prepares payloads on the training thread and performs tracker I/O on a worker thread. Flat step duration therefore does not establish that the extra timestamp gap is harmless, and timestamp gaps alone do not establish GPU idle time.

The [run tracker](https://mtracker.oa.dev/hero-run-535b) currently attributes the recurring gap to the trial build in its summary, while its September 16 03:25 entry reports the same effect in the control. The evidence above does not establish a PDL regression. The trial also changed the PJRT wheel (#9179), so the build comparison does not isolate PDL's effect on cadence.

Done when:

- Independent trainer progress timing establishes how much of the timestamp excess is real time between completed optimizer steps and how much is deferred logging.
- Measurements locate the delay within the full iteration, explain the recurring stretches, and quantify their end-to-end throughput cost against quiet periods.
- A fix, if needed, is validated across multiple slow/quiet cycles using full-iteration timing; moving time outside `throughput/duration` is insufficient.

Related: #9180 tracks checkpoint-associated spikes in measured training duration; whether it shares a cause with this pattern is unknown. #8870 tracks silent hangs, and #8506 tracks hero operations.

publicSources.title: [grug] Apply pending query bias during checkpoint evaluation
publicSources.body:
Apply a checkpoint's `pending_qb_betas` before Grug MoE evaluation callbacks run. A checkpoint-only evaluation at its stop step currently exposes the model parameters and EMA parameters without that pending update. The next normal training forward and the sampling restore path apply the update first, so evaluation can score a different routing state from the one the checkpoint would use on its next forward.

The observed score effect was small on two Hero checkpoints. It was still enough to make the first fixed-policy Paloma comparison semantically incomplete. The original `a1` results are superseded by corrected `a2` runs.

This issue is separate from the router-precision proposal in #8435. The omission occurs regardless of router dot precision. The measured impact comes from checkpoints produced by 20 steps on one B200 rack, so it does not establish the size of the effect for other checkpoints or long runs.

Requested behavior: apply the pending query-bias update to both the current and EMA model views used by evaluation hooks. Ordinary progress, logging, and checkpoint callbacks should continue to use the stored state without launching eager query-bias work.

An experimental fix and regression test exist on Romain's fork, but they have not been merged:

- Initial fix: [`2e392b6c0568e969425eb1bf97b02c853a678860`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/2e392b6c0568e969425eb1bf97b02c853a678860)
- Final scoped fix: [`a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40)
- Evaluation wrapper: [`train.py`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/blob/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L679-L693) and [eval-hook application](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/blob/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L1188-L1195)
- Regression test for current and EMA model views: [`test_eval_callback_models_apply_pending_query_bias`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/blob/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40/tests/test_moe_hero_ep.py#L361-L387)

Done when checkpoint evaluation applies the pending query-bias state to current and EMA models, the regression passes, and non-evaluation callbacks avoid this extra work.

<details><summary>Evidence and reproduction</summary>

### Observed behavior

The checkpoint stores `pending_qb_betas` separately from `params`. The training step applies those betas as centered router bias before the next forward, then stores newly computed betas for the following step. The evaluation callback model getters expose raw `params` and EMA parameters. A forced end-of-run callback at an already reached stop step can therefore evaluate the router bias embedded in the parameters and omit the pending update.

The problem appeared while comparing two step-126020 continuation checkpoints under current router arithmetic. Both checkpoints came from the same complete step-126000 native state:

`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-main-step121638/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-126000`

[`e8460b35bd6b312b62799b12ae363b3981af3c83`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/e8460b35bd6b312b62799b12ae363b3981af3c83) is the observed production source identity for that checkpoint. It does not identify the experimental continuation code.

The experiment branch was based on [`1f9c387b6c452895ff58573c2b6117c5500303db`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/1f9c387b6c452895ff58573c2b6117c5500303db). The router arithmetic controls used by the experiment were added in [`f9178348f5237cb2cb591024511d4db693a3910c`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/f9178348f5237cb2cb591024511d4db693a3910c). The corrected evaluation behavior was introduced in [`2e392b6c0568e969425eb1bf97b02c853a678860`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/2e392b6c0568e969425eb1bf97b02c853a678860) and scoped to evaluation hooks in [`a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40).

The two continuations used seed 0, the restored data-loader state, and steps 126000 through 126019:

| Checkpoint | Continuation job | W&B | Checkpoint path |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Current arithmetic | `/romain/hero-router-current-cont-coord-01a0c066-a1` | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-current-cont-step126k-01a0c066-a1) | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-training-router-01a0c066/checkpoints/current-a1/step-126020` |
| Preferred FP32 accumulation | `/romain/hero-router-pref-cont-coord-01a0c066-a1` | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-pref-cont-step126k-01a0c066-a1) | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-training-router-01a0c066/checkpoints/preferred-fp32-a1/step-126020` |

### Superseded and corrected evaluations

The `a1` jobs used raw callback model state and are superseded:

| Checkpoint | Iris job | W&B | Macro loss | Macro BPB |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Current | `/romain/hero-router-current-fixed-eval-coord-01a0c066-a1` | [superseded run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-current-fixed-eval-step126020-01a0c066-a1) | 2.22020006 | 0.80684924 |
| Preferred-trained | `/romain/hero-router-pref-fixed-eval-coord-01a0c066-a1` | [superseded run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-pref-fixed-eval-step126020-01a0c066-a1) | 2.22091150 | 0.80714315 |

The `a2` jobs applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update before the same fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation:

| Checkpoint | Iris job | W&B | Macro loss | Macro BPB |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Current | `/romain/hero-router-current-fixed-eval-qb-coord-01a0c066-a2` | [corrected run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-current-fixed-eval-qb-step126020-01a0c066-a2) | 2.22016478 | 0.80683833 |
| Preferred-trained | `/romain/hero-router-pref-fixed-eval-qb-coord-01a0c066-a2` | [corrected run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-pref-fixed-eval-qb-step126020-01a0c066-a2) | 2.22088742 | 0.80713451 |

Applying the pending state changed macro loss by `-0.00003528` for the current checkpoint and `-0.00002408` for the preferred-trained checkpoint. The preferred-minus-current macro-loss delta changed from `+0.00071144` to `+0.00072265`. This correction does not change the router investigation's recommendation, but it makes the evaluation represent the complete checkpoint state.

Both corrected jobs completed all 16 tasks without failures or preemptions. Their extracted metrics are at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-training-router-01a0c066/evidence/fixed-eval-with-pending-qb-a2.json`, SHA-256 `d13af487ee6b7f54644b9dcb5e3d7a37fdcc6e17420b7cf7476652877f8e9182`.

The final investigation report is at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-training-router-01a0c066/evidence/hero-router-training-report.md`, SHA-256 `454aae5894a78c99752cff47301441c9a8d315b30d5d1ddf1410c069bba73f4c`. The review response that prompted and verified the correction is at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-training-router-01a0c066/evidence/goal-review-response.md`, SHA-256 `a5bfff56802f87c14b6be057f4cbd9e6f86d298906071f28cbe77f532217a3d9`.

### Reproduction

Run from the experimental fork at [`a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40). Set `SOURCE` to either step-126020 checkpoint above. Because `num-steps` equals the restored state step, the optimization loop takes no step and the forced final callback runs Paloma:

```sh
python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.launch_diagnostics \
  --run-id <fixed-eval-run-id> \
  --dp-racks 1 --batch-size 1024 --optimizer-batch-size 11264 \
  --gate-router-weight-decay 0.02 --num-steps 126020 --schedule-steps 390251 \
  --initialize-from-checkpoint "${SOURCE}" --router-dot-precision current \
  --training-data mixture --eval-every 1 --version dev --run
```

The focused validation command was:

```sh
OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 nice -n 10 uv run --frozen --python 3.12 \
  pytest -n 0 --tb=short -q \
  tests/test_grug_hero_scaling_ladder.py tests/test_moe_hero_ep.py
```

Result: 71 passed, with one pre-existing JAX scatter future warning. `./infra/pre-commit.py --changed-files --fix` also passed.

</details>

publicSources.title: [fast-track] Marin Belay v1: hill-climb the scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss, 8 min on 8×H100)
publicSources.body:
This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline, clean KMA and candidate 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/9697c11ef215ec0f9d536a1bceb0876f768fcf26/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The red diamonds are the current best recipe, candidate 9 (Status below): **2.977 / 2.725 / 2.515 / 2.397** at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. d512 and d768 are seed means, and the bigram table follows rule A. d768–d1280 are data-matched; d512 sits at its fixed-time step count (2817 vs 2383 steps), so it's plotted slightly to the right. That is 0.157 / 0.098 / 0.078 / 0.074 below clean KMA. Its dash-dot curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`. Its slope is a little shallower than clean KMA's, so the gap narrows with compute: projected to **1e24 FLOPs, 1.710 vs clean KMA's 1.727, about 1.48× clean KMA's compute efficiency and 2.95× the 535B baseline's**. Because the fixed-time d512 point flattens the fitted slope, that projection is probably conservative. The right panel is clean KMA's training MFU at each rung on one 8×H100 node: 9.5% at d512 and d768, 12.2% at d1024, and 13.0% at d1280. FLOPs are counted from KMA's own layers (KDA, MLA + Inkling, AttnRes), as 3× forward with no recompute. The trainer's logged `throughput/mfu` uses the baseline architecture's FLOP formula, so it is slightly off for KMA. ## Objective **Minimize Paloma macro loss (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, final step) at the d512 rung after a fixed 8 minutes of 8×H100 train-step time.** - **Fixed time, not fixed tokens.** Faster code trains on more tokens within the 8 minutes, so a pure speedup counts as a win. - The LR schedule depends on the step count, so fix steps before each run: `num_steps = round(480 s × ex/s ÷ batch)`. - Measure ex/s with a short `--no-eval` probe (~30 steps) on the same cluster, and use the steady-state throughput. - Compile, evals and startup are excluded from the 8 minutes. - **Numerics changes are allowed** (e.g. FP8, precision changes, approximate kernels). They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. If you try a new architecture or component, tune its optimizer assignment, LR, init and other key hyperparameters before concluding it doesn't work. The baseline's settings were tuned for the baseline, not for the new idea. ## Architecture (current best, d512) The diagrams below show **clean KMA**. The current best recipe adds the components listed under **Status → Current best recipe**: MLA key norm and key offset, a gated bigram-memory AttnRes source, ReLU² experts, and optimizer, schedule and logit changes. The diagrams show d512; the other rungs differ in the Shape table only. **1. Layer stack and Block Attention Residuals.** Every sublayer reads its input through its own AttnRes gate, a per-token softmax over the residual history. At d512 each layer closes an AttnRes block, so the history at layer *i* is the embedding plus one sum per earlier layer. [¹](#arch-note) ```mermaid flowchart TB tok["token ids

🤖 **Batch 137: can the final-logit z-loss go now that we have the soft-cap? Results first, plan below.**

| run | steps | z-loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ | loss spikes (> 0.25 above the local mean) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `zl0` (2 seeds) | 2817 | 0 | 2.9758 / 2.9800 | +0.0008 / +0.0009 vs 2.9750 / 2.9791 | |
| `ot4-z` | 11268 (4×) | 1e-4 | 2.7968 | reference | 2 (steps 2834, 4854; +0.26 / +0.28) |
| `ot4-zl0` | 11268 (4×) | 0 | 2.7949 | −0.0019 | 2 (same steps, same size) |

- **Stable without z-loss, with the soft-cap, at 4× overtrain.** Both 4× runs have the same two small spikes at the same steps and recover identically. That points to the data, not missing logit control. Nothing drifted or diverged.
- **Also no gain:** +0.0009 at equal steps and −0.0019 at 4×, both within noise.
- **The decision rule's conditions are met** (4× run clean, equal steps not worse), but dropping z-loss buys nothing measurable at d512.
- **My recommendation:** leave it in, since it's cheap insurance and removing it saves ~nothing. If you'd rather simplify the recipe, the next check before gate 2 is a d768 run at 4× steps without z-loss. Your call.

---

**Plan (as posted before the runs):**


**Background:**
- The z-loss rule came from batch 17: without it "the model will blow up in the overtrain regime", so a z-loss-0 gate-2 bundle was cancelled.
- That was before the logit soft-cap. Candidate 9 caps logits at ±10 (`c·tanh(z/c)`), which bounds `log Z` directly. That's the drift the z-loss was there to stop.
- At d512, z-loss 0 alone was worth only −0.002 (batch 7, an older base).

**Test design:** a single equal-steps comparison can't test "overtrain blow-up", so there are two parts.

| arm | steps | z-loss | tests |
|---|---|---|---|
| `zl0` (2 seeds) | 2817 | 0 | the gain at the objective's scale, paired vs 2.9750 / 2.9791 |
| `ot4-z` | 11268 (4×) | 1e-4 | overtrain reference, EMA scaled (β 0.99875, last 4000 steps) |
| `ot4-zl0` | 11268 (4×) | 0 | the stress test: loss spikes and max-logit or `log Z` growth over a long run |

- **Decision rule:** drop the z-loss only if `ot4-zl0` trains as cleanly as `ot4-z` (no spikes, no divergence, final loss within noise) *and* `zl0` isn't worse. Until then the rule stays.
- **Worth noting:** 4× at d512 is an overtrain proxy, not the regime where batch 17's worry would bite hardest. If it passes, a d768 overtrain check is the next step before anything goes to gate 2.

🤖 **Batch 145: the final layers' routed experts write the full residual stream** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5923264481); d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on the same cluster, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`c6e2fa7a0b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/c6e2fa7a0b), cw-rno2a)

In candidate 9 the routed experts write a 256-wide latent, which `w_latent_up` maps to the 512-wide stream. So the routed output of every layer lies in a 256-dim subspace of the residual. If the final layers' MLPs act as predictors, that confines half the prediction space.

**Change** (`latent_out_full_layers`): in the listed layers, the routed experts' `w_down` writes `hidden_dim` directly and `w_latent_up` is dropped. Everything else is unchanged:
- the experts still read the 256 latent;
- the shared expert, the router and the other layers are untouched.

The layers live in their own stacks (`stacked_blocks_tail` / `kda_blocks_tail`); with Block AttnRes the forward already runs layer by layer. The optimizer's family patterns now include the tail stacks, so those layers get the same groups as before (tested).

| run | layers writing the full stream |
|---|---|
| `lofull5` | 5 (the final MLA layer) |
| `lofull45` | 4 and 5 (the final KDA and MLA layers) |

**Cost.** Each listed layer's expert `w_down` doubles, from I × 256 to I × 512 per expert. Its `w_latent_up` (256 × 512) is dropped. The combine moves 512-wide instead of 256-wide rows, so it costs some step time. This batch measures the ML effect at equal steps; I'll measure the step time from the same runs.

**Context.** Making the write full-width in *every* layer (latent read 256 / write 512) cost +0.0017 at data-matched d768 in an earlier batch. This tests whether the final layers are the exception.

**Relaunched** as `lof5` / `lof45` at [`f7a1e82fcd`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/f7a1e82fcd). The first runs trained normally but crashed at their first eval. The dropless eval chose the `sonic` kernel, which needs equal expert read and write widths, by looking at the global config only; it now uses `scatter` whenever `latent_out_full_layers` is set. Training is unaffected: only the eval kernel changes.

---

### Results (Paloma macro, equal steps 2817, vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a: 2.9768 / 2.9822)

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean Δ | median step | parameters | Δ at fixed time (8 min, est.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| candidate 9 | 2.9768 | 2.9822 | | 184.3 ms | 926M | |
| `lof5`: layer 5 writes the full stream | 2.9665 (−0.0103) | 2.9699 (−0.0123) | **−0.0113** | 194 ms (+5.2%) | 976M | ≈ −0.002 |
| `lof45`: layers 4 and 5 | 2.9643 (−0.0125) | 2.9661 (−0.0161) | **−0.0143** | 205 ms (+11%) | 1026M | ≈ +0.005 |

- **A large, consistent gain at equal steps.** The final layer alone gives −0.011, about twice the seed noise, and adding layer 4 brings it to −0.014. This fits the hypothesis that the final layers' MLPs predict and that the 256-dim latent write confines them.
- **It isn't free.** Each full-width layer doubles its routed experts' `w_down` (+50M parameters, 512 experts × 384 × 256) and widens the combine rows. At the measured 1% step time ≈ 0.0017 loss, `lof5` keeps a small fixed-time gain and `lof45` loses.
- **Open questions before adopting:**
  1. **Capacity vs write rank.** Part of the gain could be the extra 50M expert parameters rather than the full-rank write. The control is to keep the latent write and give layer 5's experts the same extra parameters some other way, for example a wider expert hidden dim in that layer only.
  2. **The ladder rule.** The latent is fixed at 0.5× hidden (an anti-MFU-gaming rule for this issue). These layers write at 1× hidden on the output side. This needs your call on whether a per-layer exception is allowed.
  3. **Speed.** The +5% is the combine moving 512-wide rows plus the bigger expert GEMM. It may come down with kernel work, or by applying the full write only to the routed output's final projection.
  4. **Scale.** It needs a data-matched d768 check (6929 steps).

🤖 **Batch 146: full-stream expert write in one layer at a time** (follow-up to [batch 145](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5923385781); d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`f7a1e82fcd`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/f7a1e82fcd))

Batch 145 found that letting layer 5's routed experts write the full 512-wide stream, instead of the 256 latent, gains **−0.011** at equal steps, and layers 4 + 5 together **−0.014**. This batch runs the same change in each other layer on its own, to see whether the final layer is special or whether any one layer gains about as much. In the latter case the gain would mostly be the extra expert capacity (about +50M parameters per layer), not a prediction-specific effect.

| run | full-write layer | mixer |
|---|---|---|
| `lof0` | 0 | KDA |
| `lof1` | 1 | KDA |
| `lof2` | 2 | KDA |
| `lof3` | 3 | MLA |
| `lof4` | 4 | KDA |
| (batch 145 `lof5`) | 5 | MLA, −0.0113 |

Each arm adds the same parameter count and the same step cost (about +5%), so differences between layers measure where the full-rank write matters, not how much capacity was added. ---

### Results (Paloma macro, equal steps, Δ vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; candidate 9's median step is 184.3 ms)

| full-write layer | mixer | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean Δ | median step |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | KDA | −0.0031 | −0.0030 | −0.0031 | 192 ms |
| 1 | KDA | −0.0020 | −0.0026 | −0.0023 | 193 ms |
| 2 | KDA | +0.0002 | −0.0017 | −0.0008 | 192 ms |
| 3 | MLA | −0.0049 | −0.0038 | −0.0044 | 192 ms |
| 4 | KDA | −0.0067 | −0.0083 | **−0.0075** | 192 ms |
| 5 (batch 145) | MLA | −0.0103 | −0.0123 | **−0.0113** | 194 ms |

- **The gain grows toward the output, and the final layer is the most sensitive.** Every arm adds the same about 50M expert parameters and costs the same about +4–5% step time.
  - Layers 0–2 gain −0.001 to −0.003. That is roughly what the extra capacity is worth anywhere.
  - Layer 3 gains −0.004, layer 4 −0.0075, and layer 5 −0.011: about 3–5× the early layers for the same parameters.
  - So most of the final layers' gain comes from the full-rank write, not the capacity. This supports the hypothesis that the final MLPs predict and that the 256-wide latent write confines them.
- **The MLA layer 3 gains more than its KDA neighbours** (−0.0044 vs −0.0008 for layer 2). It may matter that the global layers write to the stream differently, or it may be position (it's the 4th of 6). Only one MLA layer sits mid-stack, so position and mixer can't be separated here.
- **Layers 4 + 5 together** (batch 145: −0.0143) gain less than the sum of each alone (−0.0188). The two overlap.
- **At fixed time** (8 min, 1% step time ≈ 0.0017):
  - only layer 5 alone keeps a net gain, about −0.002;
  - layer 4 alone is about even (−0.0075 + 0.0071);
  - the early layers lose.

  Whether this is adoptable depends on cutting the step cost and on your call about the latent 0.5× rule, both raised in batch 145.

🤖 **Batch 148: drop the latent from one layer at half the expert width (parameter-matched), all 6 layers** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5924989546); d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`b2a8f69e2e`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b2a8f69e2e))

**Change** (`latent_free_layers`): in the listed layer the routed experts have no latent.
- They read the 512-wide stream directly (no `w_latent_down`) and write it directly (no `w_latent_up`).
- Their hidden width drops from 384 to 192.
- Expert parameters and FLOPs equal the latent layers': up + down is 512×192×2 = 256×384×2 per expert.
- Only the two latent projections are removed: 2 × 512 × 256 parameters per layer.

Like batch 146's full write, the layer lives in a tail stack, and the router and shared expert are unchanged.

| run | latent-free layer |
|---|---|
| `lfree0` … `lfree5` | 0, 1, 2, 3 (MLA), 4, 5 (MLA) |

**How this separates the effects:**
- Batch 146 added about 50M expert parameters per layer.
- This batch keeps expert capacity fixed, and gives the layer both full-width read and write in exchange for narrower experts.
- If the final layers gain here too, the write rank, not capacity, is what matters there.

---

### Results (Paloma macro, equal steps, Δ vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; candidate 9's median step is 184.3 ms)

| latent-free layer | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean Δ | batch 146: full write (+50M params) | median step |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 (KDA) | −0.0042 | −0.0007 | −0.0025 | −0.0031 | 194 ms |
| 1 (KDA) | −0.0009 | −0.0030 | −0.0019 | −0.0023 | 193 ms |
| 2 (KDA) | +0.0009 | +0.0006 | +0.0008 | −0.0008 | 192 ms |
| 3 (MLA) | +0.0009 | −0.0011 | −0.0001 | −0.0044 | 192 ms |
| 4 (KDA) | +0.0002 | −0.0028 | −0.0013 | −0.0075 | 194 ms |
| 5 (MLA) | −0.0022 | −0.0042 | **−0.0032** | **−0.0113** | 194 ms |

- **At matched expert parameters, removing the latent helps the final layer a little (−0.003) and the others not beyond noise.** The full-rank read and write in exchange for half the expert width is a small, final-layer-leaning gain.
- **Most of batch 145–146's final-layer gain was the extra capacity, not the write rank.**
  - Adding 50M expert parameters is worth −0.002 to −0.003 in early layers, but −0.0075 in layer 4 and −0.011 in layer 5.
  - So the final layers are where extra expert capacity pays most. The bottleneck is how much the last layers' experts can hold, more than the 256-wide write.
  - The clean next test: widen only the final layer's experts while keeping the latent (for example intermediate 384 → 768 in layer 5), with the same +50M parameters but no change to the write.
- **The step-time cost doesn't come from FLOPs.** These layers have the same expert FLOPs as candidate 9 and still take 192–194 ms (+4–5%).
  - The cost comes from moving a layer into its own tail stack, which matches the GPU 0 waiting in batch 149's profiles.
  - Fixing that overhead, so a per-layer variant doesn't cost +4% for structure alone, is now the main implementation task before any of these can be adopted.

🤖 **Batch 150: more capacity or more compute in the final layers** (follow-up to batches [146](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5924287655) and [148](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5925057549); d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`08dcf711d2`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/08dcf711d2))

**What we know so far:**
- Batch 148: at matched expert parameters, removing the latent from layer 5 gains only −0.003.
- Batch 146: adding about 50M expert parameters gains far more in layers 4–5 (−0.0075, −0.011) than early (−0.002 to −0.003).

So the open question is whether the last layers want more expert **parameters** or more **active compute**, with the latent write unchanged. Two new tail modes:
- `wide_expert_layers` / `wide_expert_intermediate_dim`: the listed layers' experts get a wider hidden dim. The latent read and write are unchanged.
- `topk_layers` / `topk_layer_k`: the listed layers activate more experts per token, at the same parameters. This was your suggestion; it is an exception to the top-8 rule in those layers only.

| run | change | extra expert params | extra active expert FLOPs in the layer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `wide5` | layer 5 experts 384 → 576 | +50M (same as batch 145 `lof5`) | ×1.5 |
| `wide45` | layers 4 and 5 at 576 | +100M | ×1.5 each |
| `top12` | layer 5 top-12 | 0 | ×1.5 |
| `top16` | layer 5 top-16 | 0 | ×2 |

**How to read it:**
- `wide5` and `top12` add the same compute to layer 5. One adds parameters, the other activates more existing experts.
- `lof5` (batch 145, −0.011) also adds +50M params and ×1.5 expert FLOPs in layer 5. So `lof5`, `wide5` and `top12` all cost the same compute, and `lof5` vs `wide5` differs only in where the extra parameters go: the output (write) width or the hidden width.

**Batch 149, all-rank profiles.** The levanter profiler traced every process, but processes on one node uploaded over each other's file, so earlier runs kept only one GPU's trace. It now uploads one session per process. `prof2-c9` and `prof2-lof5` rerun the profiles to find which GPU the others wait for.

**Results** (final Paloma macro loss; Δ vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; step = median `throughput/duration`, candidate 9 ≈ 171.6 ms on the flat step)

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `wide5` | 2.9715 (-0.0053) | — | 190.2 (+3%) |
| `wide45` | 2.9698 (-0.0070) | 2.9733 (-0.0089) | ≈198 (+8%) |
| `top12` | 2.9757 (-0.0011) | 2.9814 (-0.0008) | ≈193 (+5%) |
| `top16` | 2.9762 (-0.0006) | 2.9801 (-0.0021) | ≈198 (+8%) |

Step times are on the pre-flat-step code, where candidate 9 is ≈184 ms. `wide5` seed 1 crashed at step 1537 (cluster churn).

**Takeaway.**
- Wider final-layer experts gain at equal steps: −0.005 for layer 5, −0.007 / −0.009 for layers 4+5. At fixed time the +3% / +8% step cost cancels most of it (1% ≈ 0.0017).
- More active experts in the final layer (top-12, top-16) are within noise at +5% / +8%.
- Of the final-layer capacity options, full-width write (`lof5`, −0.0097 at +2.6% on the flat step) has the best gain per millisecond, and it's what candidate 10 uses.

🤖 **Batches 152, 157, 160: host dispatch, and pipelining the train loop** (runtime only, no ML change; d512 candidate 9 + PGLE on cw-rno2a)

**Goal:** remove host time from the step. Batch 149's profiles showed every GPU waiting on process 0 to launch each step.

**152, flat-leaves train step** ([`a99a1ef88b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a99a1ef88b) and earlier on `ladderclimb_v1_lc1`)
- **Change:** the step is jitted over the train state's flat list of arrays rather than the equinox tree. That avoids Python flattening the whole module tree on every call (26–40 ms per step at d512, with the GPUs idle).

| run | steps | final Paloma macro | Δ vs candidate 9 | median step (`throughput/duration`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [lc1-b152-flat](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b152-flat) | 2817 | 2.9773 | +0.0005 (same math) | 171.6 ms, vs 184.3 for candidate 9 (**−6.9%**) |
| [lc1-b152-flat-lof5](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b152-flat-lof5), with full write on layer 5 | 2817 | **2.9676** | −0.0092 | 176.1 ms (+2.6% vs flat candidate 9) |

**157 and 160, pipelined loop** (`--pipeline-depth`; [`aa1c82fb35`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/aa1c82fb35), [`17dd004ca0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/17dd004ca0), [`a1d76fcc23`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a1d76fcc23))
- **Change:** step n+1 is dispatched before the host waits on step n, so logging and callbacks overlap the GPUs.
- **Measurement fix:** `throughput/duration` measures dispatch to loss-ready. It leaves out about 20 ms of host time between steps, so wall-clock per step (from wandb timestamps) was **191 ms for the flat step, not 171.6**.
- **First version (157):** a device-side NaN check queued behind the next step, so it saved only 4 ms (187 ms wall-clock). Its full run, [lc1-b157-pipe](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b157-pipe), is 2.9777, so the loop doesn't change the math.
- **Fixed version (`pipe2`), 300-step timing:** lof5 at **171.2 ms wall-clock vs 195.8** without pipelining (−12.6%).
- **But full-length runs crash.** Every one died between steps 512 and 515 (`CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` / `LAUNCH_FAILED`), across features and seeds. Batch 160 bisected it at 700 steps:

| run | pipeline | PGLE | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| lc1-b160-p1 | depth 1 | on | crashed |
| lc1-b160-p1-nopgle | depth 1 | off | crashed |
| lc1-b160-p0 | depth 0 | on | completed |

- **Status:** fully overlapping consecutive steps causes the crash; PGLE doesn't. Root cause not found yet, so `--pipeline-depth` now defaults to 0 ([`f4d76bf53a`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/f4d76bf53a)).
- **What it's worth under our rule:** `throughput/duration` already excludes the host gap, so pipelining mostly makes wall-clock match the metric (191 → 171 ms). The flat step's −6.9% is the gain that counts, worth ≈ −0.012 at fixed time (1% ≈ 0.0017).

**Toward candidate 10** (flat step + full write on the final layer, or final 2):
- **161:**
  - `c10-s1`, lof5 seed 1 (seed 0 is 2.9676 above);
  - `prof`, a no-PGLE profile with the HLO dump from the same compile, to attribute the 74 ms of elementwise/reduce kernels per step;
  - d768 validation, `d768-c9` vs `d768-lof7` (the last layer, 6929 steps).
- **162:** `lof45` on two seeds (layers 4+5 gained −0.014 at equal steps in batch 145, before the flat step), plus 300-step timing of `lof45` vs candidate 9 on the flat step.

Results will be edited into this comment.

publicSources.title: [iris] Decide whether jobs may require a named NVLink rack
publicSources.body:
## TL;DR

- **Decision:** Should an Iris Kubernetes job be able to require one specific NVLink rack?
- **Need:** `group_by="nvlink.domain"` keeps a gang in one rack but does not choose which rack. A job limited to rack 392 needs to name it.
- **Current gap:** Iris skips that exact-rack constraint when building a Kubernetes Pod and lowercases the case-sensitive rack label before serialization.
- **Proposal:** [Draft PR #9478](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9478) would let a job require `nvlink.domain == "DH1-392-US-EAST-08A"`. The job could not run on another rack if the requested rack is missing or full.
- **Scope:** This feature would not reserve Hero training racks or prevent Batch jobs from using spare nodes there.

A read-only audit on September 26 found three Batch jobs using 24 GPUs on six other nodes in three of Hero's 11 training racks. It found no GPU double-booking and did not measure training harm. No placement with the changed controller has been tested live.

<details>
<summary>Evidence: placement audit, current code, and a local test failure</summary>

**Placement audit.** Iris controller `task_attempts` showed Hero using 16 nodes on each of 11 racks (176 four-GPU tasks). Racks 124, 125, and 129 each had 18 labeled nodes: 16 used by Hero and two by one Batch job. Captured Kubernetes node labels mapped the nodes to racks; FineLog `iris.profile` samples confirmed the Batch tasks ran there. The audit did not compare training speed with and without Batch work. A separate job requested only `group_by="nvlink.domain"`, so its placement did not test an exact-rack request.

**Actual rack label.** The captured Kubernetes node snapshot included `s1mwxs64` with `ds.coreweave.com/nvlink.domain=DH1-392-US-EAST-08A`. The uppercase characters matter for an exact label match.

**Current code.** [Gang topology](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/562d705673859548c58b46d8f2383ab8a053797f/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L285-L292) selects the `nvlink.domain` level without a rack value. The [Pod selector mapping](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/562d705673859548c58b46d8f2383ab8a053797f/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L179-L183) lists only `pool` and `region`; [unknown keys are skipped](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/562d705673859548c58b46d8f2383ab8a053797f/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L335-L346). [String constraints are lowercased](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/562d705673859548c58b46d8f2383ab8a053797f/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/constraints.py#L106-L110) before they are sent.

**Local reproduction.** Adding only the missing Pod mapping produced this failure for an illustrative uppercase rack label. It shows why the label's case must also survive serialization:

```text
assert manifest["spec"]["nodeSelector"]["ds.coreweave.com/nvlink.domain"] == rack
E AssertionError: assert 'dh1-001-us-east-08a' == 'DH1-001-US-EAST-08A'
```

The [draft PR's regression test](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a30e700ae2cc164e28b8f244a8fe9a65f8584454/lib/iris/tests/cluster/backends/k8s/test_pod_manifest.py#L681-L693) checks that the exact label survives controller storage and reaches the Pod's selector and required affinity.

</details>

publicSources.title: [evaluation] Make one-sample generation runs repeatable
publicSources.body:
Two full runs of the same frozen Snowball parent produced different coding scores, although their artifact model configs are equal and the Evalchemy config sets `seed: 42`.

| Benchmark | Run `2026.09.29.1` | Run `2026.09.29.7` | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| HumanEval+ | 51.83% | 42.07% | -9.76 points |
| MBPP+ | 42.06% | 44.18% | +2.12 points |
| CRUXEval input | 4.63% | 4.00% | -0.63 point |
| CRUXEval output | 8.88% | 7.63% | -1.25 points |

Both artifacts use:

- `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-GLM53-RLVR-SFT-2026.09.23@227263f32121ac79ba96de6136b86221e58b05db`
- the same tokenizer revision
- an 8,192-token generation limit
- `skip_special_tokens=false` and `repetition_penalty=1.1`
- the same serving topology
- the `coding-expert-code` evaluation with seed 42 and thinking off

Artifacts:

- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/snowball-python-expert-parent/coding-expert-code/2026.09.29.1`
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/snowball-python-expert-parent/coding-expert-code/2026.09.29.7`

The likely cause is that Evalchemy's launch seed does not set a fixed sampler seed for each OpenAI request. The code evaluation also has no explicit temperature, so the endpoint can use its sampling default. Confirm the request payload before selecting a fix.

One sampled answer per item can change enough to alter a model comparison. A recorded launch seed does not currently prove that a repeated generation run is deterministic.

This was found during #9528. Its temporary workaround is to run the frozen parent and candidate together, compare only that matched pair, and report paired task-level intervals. Do not compare the candidate to the earlier parent artifact. All four paired coding intervals in the matched run include zero, so the spike does not use the higher candidate point estimate as promotion evidence.

Done when:

1. Define the canonical sampler behavior for one-sample generation evaluations. Use an explicit deterministic temperature or derive and send a stable request seed from the task, document ID, and repeat index.
2. Store the effective request sampling values in the result provenance.
3. Add a repeatability check that runs the same small generated-task panel twice and compares the sample outputs.
4. Run the frozen parent twice after the fix and confirm equal outputs or document the expected variance when deterministic serving is not possible.

---

publicSources.body:
## Overview

This living policy defines which evaluation results for Marin models and comparison baselines are reportable, public-facing, and canonical. It records the evaluations, their hyperparameters and experimental constraints, and the self-contained codebase needed to reproduce the results independently. The policy is intended to be a trustworthy snapshot for each period in which it applies.

The first Snowball 67B A2B MoE release brings regular comparisons with existing open and closed-source models. Marin's open-development claim requires transparent reporting of evaluation scores and the capability claims based on them.

## Previous version notes

* Released Sept 24, 2026: 18 non-agentic benchmarks, 8 Harbor agentic benchmarks, and 4 reserved out-of-distribution benchmarks.

## Complete eval list, with hyperparameters

### In Distribution

Runtime statistics use the completed, tracker-linked runs from this campaign and report the sample
standard deviation across models. Evalchemy and lm-eval-harness runtimes span the Iris evaluator
task's recorded start and finish. Harbor runtimes span the benchmark job's `started_at` and
`finished_at`; for policy-valid partial seals, the final `updated_at` at sealing is used instead.
Scheduler wait and model-server startup are excluded. The table should be refreshed when the
remaining NUPA, SWE-bench Verified, and τ³ cells seal.

### Out of Distribution

* AAII 4.3
* Terminal-Bench Science
* DeepSWE 1.1 (deep-swe-litecontainer@1.1)

### Details on our Evals

- **MATH-500.** OpenAI's [May 2023 process-supervision release](https://openai.com/index/improving-mathematical-reasoning-with-process-supervision/) used a 500-problem subset of the original MATH competition-math benchmark. The campaign scores one zero-shot generated solution per problem by final-answer accuracy.
- **HumanEval+.** The [May 2023 EvalPlus paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01210) introduced expanded tests for HumanEval programs to catch incorrect code that passes sparse original tests. The campaign executes one zero-shot completion per problem against the stronger tests.
- **MBPP+.** The [November 24, 2023 EvalPlus release](https://github.com/evalplus/evalplus/releases/tag/v0.2.0) extends MBPP with additional functional tests. The campaign's pinned config is zero-shot and scores one generated program per problem.
- **OlympiadBench.** The [February 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14008) introduced bilingual, multimodal Olympiad-level math and science problems. This campaign uses Evalchemy's 30-question text subset, ten sampled solutions per question, and the configured answer judge.
- **GSM8K.** The [October 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168) introduced grade-school math word problems requiring multi-step arithmetic. The campaign uses the zero-shot `gsm8k-0shot` completion route and scores the extracted final answer.
- **PIQA.** The [November 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.11641) introduced two-choice questions about physical commonsense. The campaign selects the answer by length-normalized log-likelihood with no examples in the prompt.
- **WinoGrande.** The [July 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.10641) introduced adversarial pronoun/coreference choices designed to reduce superficial cues. The campaign uses five-shot multiple-choice scoring.
- **BoolQ.** The [May 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10044) introduced naturally occurring yes/no questions paired with evidence passages. The campaign scores zero-shot choice accuracy.
- **TruthfulQA MC2.** The [September 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.07958) introduced questions that elicit common misconceptions from language models. The campaign's MC2 metric sums probability mass on all true answers within each question's candidate set, rather than counting a single selected answer.
- **TriviaQA.** The [May 2017 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.03551) introduced trivia questions with independently collected evidence documents. The campaign runs five-shot answer generation and reports answer accuracy.
- **AIME24.** The [Mathematical Association of America's 2024 AIME](https://maa.org/maa-invitational-competitions/) supplies the contest problems. Evalchemy samples ten solutions per question in one run through the shared seeded-repeat implementation and scores the integer final answers.
- **MMLU-Pro.** The [June 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01574) introduced harder, more reasoning-focused multiple-choice questions across fourteen subjects. The campaign runs zero-shot generation with a 65,536-token cap and reports micro-averaged accuracy.
- **GPQA Diamond.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12022) introduced expert-written graduate-level science questions, including the Diamond subset. The campaign averages accuracy over three generated answers per question.
- **CRUXEval (output).** The [January 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03065) introduced input- and output-prediction tasks for short Python programs. The tracker reports the output-prediction direction, scored on one generated answer per item.
- **FinanceBench.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11944) introduced questions grounded in public financial filings. The campaign scores one generated answer per question with its pinned LLM judge.
- **IFBench.** The [July 2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02833) introduced verifiable constraints that test generalization in precise instruction following. The campaign reports strict prompt-level accuracy, requiring every constraint to hold in the raw response.
- **MRCR.** [Gemini's September 2024 report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640) introduced multi-round coreference resolution; [OpenAI's public MRCR release (April 2025)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/mrcr) supplies the corrected multi-needle data used here. The campaign scores nonce-gated sequence similarity and selects only context-length bins that fit the served model.
- **NUPA stratified (Loose).** The [November 2024 Number Cookbook paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.03766) introduced tests of numerical understanding and processing across representations and tasks. The campaign uses Evalchemy's pinned `NUPA5K-Loose` benchmark: a deterministic 5,000-record stratified sample covering 44 tasks and 2,391 strata, scored with permissive answer extraction rather than the paper's direct-answer protocol. Its longest rendered prompt is 399 tokens under Evalchemy's reference tokenizer; the standard 256-token prompt cushion and 64-token endpoint guard leave a 72,945-token response cap inside the 73,664-token single-turn context window.
- **SWE-bench Verified.** OpenAI's [August 13, 2024 release](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/) introduced the 500-task, human-validated repository-issue repair set. The campaign runs Harbor's canonical `swebench-verified@1.0` implementation with mini-swe-agent 2.1.0, one trial per issue, and executable verification.
- **OpenThoughts-TBLite 2.0.** The [February 18, 2026 release](https://www.openthoughts.ai/blog/openthoughts-tblite) introduced a 100-task, faster-running terminal-agent panel calibrated against Terminal-Bench 2. The campaign runs its pinned `openthoughts-tblite@2.0` tasks with Terminus-2, three trials per task, and reports mean verifier success across trials.
- **Terminal-Bench 2.1.** The [November 7, 2025 release](https://www.tbench.ai/news/announcement-2-0) introduced a harder, more thoroughly verified terminal-agent task set alongside Harbor. The campaign uses `terminal-bench/terminal-bench-2-1` at ref 6 through Harbor, with three Terminus-2 trials per task, a 65,536-token context window, and a 16,384-token per-turn output cap.
- **DS-1000 mini-200.** The [November 2022 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.11501) introduced data-science code-generation problems spanning seven Python libraries. The campaign evaluates a fixed seed-42 200-task Harbor subset with Terminus-2, building task images from the pinned Dockerfiles.
- **BFCL-Parity @ Pi.** Berkeley's [February 2024 BFCL release](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/blogs/8_berkeley_function_calling_leaderboard.html) introduced executable function-calling evaluation. This campaign uses the Harbor `bfcl_parity@1.0` adaptation with the Pi agent, so its score is the pinned adaptation's verified solve rate rather than an unqualified BFCL leaderboard score.
- **BixBench CLI corrections @ Pi.** The [February 2025 BixBench paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00096) introduced multi-step computational-biology analysis tasks. This campaign uses Pi on 205 `bixbench-cli-marin-corrections@3` tasks and reports binary answer-equivalence reward, which is distinct from canonical BixBench CLI v1.5.
- **τ³-bench @ Pi.** Sierra's [March 18, 2026 τ³-Bench launch](https://sierra.ai/blog/bench-advancing-agent-benchmarking-to-knowledge-and-voice) introduced knowledge and voice tracks alongside corrections to the existing airline and retail tasks. The campaign runs pinned `tau3-bench@1.0.1` in Harbor through the Pi ACP relay and scores task verification.
- **SOTOPIA-hard.** The [October 2023 SOTOPIA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11667) introduced interactive social-agent evaluation and identified a hard scenario subset. The campaign runs the 100 hard episodes against a fixed `openai/gpt-oss-120b` counterpart and judge, then normalizes goal achievement from 0–10 to 0–1.

### How do we handle in-distribution and out-of-distribution evals?

#### IN-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- dedup against our SFT data, look at model scores while we develop the model, inspect the correlation of our ID evals with our OOD evals

**We may** -- develop synthetic RL tasks modeled on specific tasks in ID evals

**We will not** -- train on teacher rollouts from eval questions, use our ID eval instructions directly as the basis of RL data

#### OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- de-dup against our SFT raw data, look at meta-data about these evals (e.g., how big they are, general knowledge domain, etc), eval baselines on these evals

**We may** -- evaluate our final models on out-of-distribution benchmarks

**We will not** -- look at the individual questions in the evals, look at any of our own model scores from these evals until our model is frozen, model any synthetic tasks on tasks in the evals (edited)

### Metric definitions

- **`accuracy`:** the fraction of scored items that pass the benchmark's configured correctness check. The common name covers executable-test success for code and agent tasks, answer correctness for generated and multiple-choice tasks, FinanceBench's `correct` judge label, and BixBench's binary answer-equivalence check. NUPA Loose applies format-specific, permissive answer extraction before a representation-sensitive exact match. PIQA chooses the option with the highest length-normalized log-likelihood before testing correctness. AIME24 and OlympiadBench average ten seeded samples per item; GPQA Diamond averages three. MMLU-Pro is micro-averaged across its fourteen subjects.
- **`mc2`:** TruthfulQA's probability mass on all true answers, normalized over the question's answer set and averaged over questions. It is not a binary selection accuracy, and chance performance is above zero.
- **`accuracy (output)`:** CRUXEval output-prediction accuracy. Given a function and input, the model predicts the output; this is distinct from CRUXEval input prediction, which reconstructs an input from the function and desired output.
- **`strict prompt-level accuracy`:** the fraction of IFBench prompts for which the raw response satisfies every required constraint.
- **`mean sequence similarity`:** MRCR's mean `SequenceMatcher` ratio between the response's answer span and the reference answer. A response that fails MRCR's nonce check receives zero credit. The standard 73,728-token serving window evaluates the published bins through 65,536 tokens. After Marin's 64-token serving safety margin, the 32,768-token models use bins through 16,384 and the 65,536-token model uses bins through 32,768. Those tracker cells are footnoted because differing bin coverage is not a strictly like-for-like comparison.
- **`normalized goal achievement`:** SOTOPIA-hard's official goal-achievement score for the evaluated character, linearly normalized from `[0, 10]` to `[0, 1]` and averaged over the 100 official hard episodes. The counterpart and evaluator are fixed to `openai/gpt-oss-120b` on Together for every model.

### Other Metric Notes

- **Scale:** every metric in the suite is reported on a 0-1 scale with 1 the best and 0 the worst; there are no error counts, ranks, or unbounded scores.
- **Allowed context length:** This is allowed prompt + completion context length. If a model's maximum context length is less than the allowed context length, we adopt the model's maximum context length. For single-turn benchmarks, we subdivide the space into max prompt length = longest prompt in the dataset plus a bit of cushion, max response length = the remaining context window. For standard multi-turn benchmarks, max generation length per turn is capped at 8192. Context-ablation labels are `context window / per-turn output limit`: both values are passed explicitly, with the first applied to vLLM `max_model_len` and Pi `model_info.max_input_tokens`, and the second applied to Pi `model_info.max_output_tokens`. For example, `65k-16k` means a 65,536-token serving and Pi context window with a 16,384-token per-turn output limit.
- **Pi runtime:** Agentic Pi configs must pin `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` explicitly. The corrected context control pins Pi `0.87.0`; the original harness result used unpinned Pi `0.86.1`, while the first context-ablation rerun drifted to unpinned Pi `0.87.0`. Results from different Pi versions are not treated as a controlled context-only comparison.

### LLM judges

Five evals involve an LLM judge; every other eval in the suite grades programmatically
(IFBench verifies each constraint with its checker functions, MRCR uses `SequenceMatcher`,
the math evals use Minerva/SymPy, the multiple-choice evals compare selections, and the
remaining harness/agentic evals run test suites).

- **FinanceBench:** every scored response is judged. The judge sees the question, the
  reference answers, and the candidate, and returns one label: `correct`, `incorrect`, or
  `not_attempted` (equivalent answers in substance count as correct — algebraic equivalence,
  unit conversions, rounding). Only `correct` scores.
- **BixBench CLI correction set:** every submitted answer is judged for semantic equivalence
  to the task's ideal answer and receives a binary reward. A missing answer receives zero
  without invoking the judge.
- **OlympiadBench:** Minerva/SymPy grades first, and the judge answers equivalence only for
  answers Minerva cannot establish; the reported scores come from the offline regrade, which
  uses this judge the same way (see "OlympiadBench regrade" below).
- **SOTOPIA-hard:** the official episode evaluator judges goal achievement for the evaluated
  character after each completed social interaction and returns the 0–10 score that the metric
  normalizes to 0–1.
- **τ³-bench:** the verifier combines deterministic task checks with an LLM evaluator for
  natural-language assertions. The separately configured LLM that simulates the user is part of
  the task environment, not the judge.

Judge deployment is benchmark-specific:

- **FinanceBench and OlympiadBench** use `openai/gpt-oss-120b` through Together. The launch
  configuration supplies `JUDGE_MODEL`, `JUDGE_BASE_URL`, and a Together API key.
- **BixBench** uses a co-hosted `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8` judge at revision
  `c5454eb03678d8710e54a4e0fc681b9f3b4a3dba`. Marin serves it on eight H100s with tensor
  parallelism 8, a 32,768-token context window, the `minimax_m3` reasoning parser, prefix
  caching, and CUDA graphs enabled. The verifier receives the co-hosted endpoint and model
  identity directly from Marin; it does not use the Together judge environment.
- **SOTOPIA-hard** uses `openai/gpt-oss-120b` through Together for both the fixed counterpart
  and the official episode evaluator. Its LiteLLM identifier is
  `openai/openai/gpt-oss-120b`: the first segment selects the OpenAI-compatible provider and
  the remainder is Together's model ID.
- **τ³-bench** uses that same Together-hosted model and LiteLLM identifier for both the user
  simulator and the natural-language assertion evaluator. The two roles are independently
  configured even though this campaign pins them to the same checkpoint.

Judge hyperparameters, per path:

- **Answer-equivalence judge** (FinanceBench, OlympiadBench): a single user message with the
  three-way rubric, `temperature=0`, request timeout 300 s with 5 transport retries, and 16
  concurrent judgments per run. `max_tokens` starts at 128 and escalates 128 → 512 → 2048
  when a completion comes back empty — a hosted reasoning model can spend a small completion
  budget on hidden reasoning and return no content — so the ladder guarantees the final label
  lands within budget. The context window is gpt-oss-120b's 131,072 tokens as served
  (Together); no truncation of the graded material happens judge-side. The raw completion is
  retained in the results for audit, alongside the parsed label.
- **BixBench verifier:** the verifier calls the co-hosted MiniMax Chat Completions endpoint
  with `max_tokens=1024` and a structured response schema containing one boolean score.
  Sampling follows the endpoint's service defaults.
- **SOTOPIA evaluator:** the pinned SOTOPIA v0.1.5 evaluator uses the fixed judge model after
  each episode; the model under evaluation never acts as its own judge.
- **τ³ natural-language assertions:** the pinned τ³ adapter passes only assertions that need
  semantic evaluation to its configured LLM; deterministic assertions remain programmatic.

When a judge call fails after retries, the sample is recorded as grader infrastructure
failure (counted against the run's error tolerance) rather than silently scored zero.

### Thinking mode

The main table records the policy for every benchmark. `on` and `off` set
`enable_thinking` through the model or benchmark config; a benchmark override wins over the model
default. `model default` means the benchmark adds no override, and `not applicable` means the task
does not use a generated chat response. If a model cannot turn reasoning off (e.g. GPT-OSS), an `off` benchmark
uses the model's lowest available reasoning setting instead.

### Errors and Exceptions

#### Infrastructure Error Tolerance

An evaluation may be sealed as soon as at least 90% of its declared trials have valid scores under
the campaign configuration. Up to 10% of declared trials may be absent because of infrastructure
failures; the result does not need to wait for those trials to be recovered. Reported uncertainty
must include this infrastructure-failure tolerance. Task-level outcomes, including agent timeouts
recorded as scores of zero, are scored trials rather than infrastructure failures.

#### Zero-score trace audit

A score of exactly zero shall be reported only after agent review of at least ten representative
traces, or every trace when the evaluation has fewer than ten. The review will check model output,
harness parsing, verifier output, and serving or sandbox errors and accept the zero when the traces support model or task failure and no untracked infrastructure failure explains the result. Otherwise, the result should be rejected and re-run under the policy.

#### Infrastructure vs Model Error

We categorize errors during the evaluation process as either infrastructure errors or model errors.
Model errors are scoreable and do not count toward the infrastructure-error threshold. Unless this
policy explicitly identifies an error as a model error, it is an infrastructure error.

##### Harbor

For Harbor evals, the following error types are currently treated as score-able model errors.

- `AgentTimeoutError`: the agent reached its configured execution timeout; Harbor preserves
  the work produced so far and runs the verifier.
- `ContextLengthExceededError`: the model or agent exhausted the available context; Harbor
  treats that as a classified end to the attempt and runs the verifier.

For these Harbor score-able model errors, we terminate the trial and then run the verifier on the output of the agent, if any output is present. Unlike the Evalchemy timeout rule above, we do *not* automatically score Harbor model errors as 0's. This is because sometimes, agents will solve the task correctly and then get stuck in a loop of self-doubt or fail to submit properly in their harness, and we regard that outcome as closer to a success than a failure.

##### Ambiguous Harbor Errors

- `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError`: the agent process exited non-zero after potentially producing scoreable work. We treat these errors as score-able but if a trial returns more than 30% NonZeroAgentExitCodeError the agent or human executing the policy should review the traces to look for infrastructure errors and invalidate the run if any are discovered.

##### Evalchemy

Under the current Evalchemy pin, `malformed_model_response` is the only named error category that
remains scoreable. It means the model endpoint returned a response that Evalchemy could not parse,
or returned no usable final-answer content. Evalchemy substitutes an empty generation, preserves
the diagnostic category, and lets the benchmark grade that generation normally; this will usually,
but not necessarily, score zero.

`AgentTimeoutError`, `model_transport`, and `grader_infrastructure` are currently serialized with
the `EVALCHEMY_INFRASTRUCTURE_ERROR` marker and excluded from scored coverage. They therefore count
against the 10% infrastructure-failure allowance rather than as zero-valued model outcomes. Other
task-level failures, including `generation_policy`, `generation`, `grading`, `serialization`,
`incomplete_evaluation`, and `invalid_result`, do not produce a scoreable trial.

This exposes a mismatch with the intended Evalchemy timeout rule below: the release policy says an
`AgentTimeoutError` should score `0.0`, but the current pinned implementation treats it as
infrastructure. Results and coverage from this pin must follow the recorded implementation behavior;
making Evalchemy timeouts scoreable requires a new code pin and provenance.



#### Timeout Policy

The following limits apply to every policy benchmark; there are no benchmark-specific exceptions.

| Evaluator phase | Limit | Outcome when the limit expires |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Evalchemy trial | 30 minutes | Record `0.0` as an `AgentTimeoutError`. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor agent setup | 6 minutes | Record `AgentSetupTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |
| Harbor agent execution | 30 minutes | Record `AgentTimeoutError`, preserve the agent's work, and run the verifier. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor verifier | 5 minutes | Record `VerifierTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |

The Evalchemy limit covers the full trial, including request retries and backoff, after the trial
acquires an evaluator slot.

Harbor launch configs override task-manifest values with
`agents[].override_setup_timeout_sec: 360`, `agents[].override_timeout_sec: 1800`, and
`verifier.override_timeout_sec: 300`. The repository-owned campaign validator checks these values
before submission, so the same limits apply even when a task manifest omits its own timeout.

## Baseline Models

### How we select baseline models

The process for selecting baseline models in our policy is fundamentally heuristic and community-driven. For each new model release, we will strive to select a representative cohort of open-weights and open-source models that are roughly comparable to Marin models and document them in the policy. We will look up reported results for those models in the research literature and, where available, use them as targets for internal reproduction, noting, however, that typically the variance in hyperparameters will make published results not directly comparable to our own. We will sometimes substitute quantized variants of the listed models for the canonical models, especially for larger models where our hardware makes it challenging to run inference on the non-quantized variants.

Launch and validation do not read configs, scripts, pins, or state from the experiment workspace.
External inputs are limited to credentials and immutable model and dataset references declared by
the checked-in configs.

### Configuration immutability

The launcher does not alter model-serving settings or benchmark semantics. It may resolve
credentials, cluster placement, output locations, concurrency, and other operational values.
Model-specific chat templates are the sole model-config composition step: a version-controlled
template under the campaign directory is inserted into the effective model YAML. The campaign YAML
also applies its checked-in, model-specific Harbor context and compaction values. Each durable run
record preserves the effective model configuration, evaluator configuration, code revision, and
Harbor policy digest. Any other semantic change requires a new checked-in config and code revision.

workspace.

## Eval launch commands (Marin)

These commands require access to the `marin` Iris controller and the `cw-rno2a` federated cluster.
