required credentials, snapshots the effective command and configs, and submits one shared-serving
root. It deliberately supplies no eval-policy label.

## Eval launch commands (Standalone)

The standalone path uses the same checked-out Marin campaign directory as the commands above. It
requires an OpenAI-compatible endpoint reachable from both the local evaluator
and Daytona sandboxes and served with the checkpoint, vLLM flags, topology, and sampling settings

must match the name returned by `/models`; `TOKENIZER_ID` is the Hugging Face repository and

## Run resumption

Resume an interrupted Harbor run only when its model, checked-out repository revision, runtime
limit, and dataset state are unchanged. Read the original run ID and effective configuration from
its durable `record.json`. Use the model and Harbor config from the same Marin commit, then add the
original run ID:

```bash
uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model-config "$CAMPAIGN/model-configs/<model-config>.yaml" \
  --harbor-config "$STAGED_HARBOR_DIR/<harbor-config>.yaml" \
  --resume-run-id <original-run-id>
```

The durable `<records-prefix>/<original-run-id>/results/harbor_jobs/` tree must remain accessible.
Harbor preserves completed scored trials and reruns missing attempts and exceptions in its pinned
resume taxonomy. Use a clean replacement when model, policy, pins, limits, records prefix, or
dataset state changed, or when the unscored error is outside that taxonomy. Never delete a trial
directory to force recovery.

## Baseline-specific launch settings

The YAML files under
`experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/model-configs/` are authoritative for checkpoint and tokenizer
revisions, serving context, GPU count, tensor and data parallelism, reasoning parser, tool parser,
sampling overrides, and Pi `thinking_format`. Use the matching file unchanged. Pi uses
`qwen-chat-template` for Qwen3.6 and Qwen3-Next and `chat-template` for the other models.

MRCR serves at 73,728 tokens and gives Evalchemy 73,664 after its 64-token safety margin. Ling
Lite's native 32,768-token window uses `mrcr-32k.yaml`; the historical 65,536-token Snowball
candidate uses `mrcr-65k.yaml`; every release-figure model uses `mrcr.yaml` otherwise. Evalchemy
evaluates only the published bins that fit.

## Updating codebase pins

Use the newest campaign pin for each codebase across the full release, assuming forward
compatibility with earlier score-producing runs. If a pin change causes an observed result
regression, stop launches, fix or revert the change, and issue a new policy version when the
evaluation behavior intentionally changes. Preserve the original run's exact pins in its immutable
config snapshot even after the release-wide pins advance.

## Standards for presenting Marin evals

* Select the release Snowball checkpoint by simple paired benchmark win rate among Snowball candidates. Release figures include only the selected checkpoint, not the other Snowball candidates. The Snowball candidate family includes the Grug 67B A2B checkpoint as well as checkpoints named Snowball. For each benchmark, plot the selected Snowball checkpoint and every non-Snowball baseline with an available score and total-training-FLOP estimate. Performance is on the y-axis and total training FLOPs are on a logarithmic x-axis. A baseline with an incomplete suite may appear in the scatterplots for its completed benchmarks, but it is excluded from cross-benchmark critical-difference analysis unless it has the full common benchmark panel.
* Produce uncertainty-aware normalized critical-difference diagrams with and without a FLOP control. Normalize scores within each benchmark across the complete-panel cohort. Estimate each score's task-level sample SEM from the scored trial rewards, then multiply the SEM by `1 / sqrt(0.9)` to account conservatively for the policy's 10% infrastructure-failure tolerance. With a fixed random seed, draw 100,000 score panels from independent normal sampling distributions centered on the reported scores and clipped to the metric's `[0, 1]` range. Rank models within every benchmark for each draw, using average ranks for ties, and report mean ranks with simultaneous 95% bands based on the draw-wise maximum absolute rank deviation. Report the Nemenyi critical difference at `alpha = 0.05`; it depends on the number of models and benchmarks, while score uncertainty affects the simulated rank distribution and its simultaneous bands.
* For the FLOP-controlled diagram, regress the draw's benchmark-normalized scores on `log10(total training FLOPs)` with one common linear slope, rank the within-benchmark residuals, and otherwise use the same uncertainty procedure. Treat FLOP estimates as fixed point estimates and disclose that their estimation uncertainty is not propagated. The uncontrolled diagram ranks the sampled normalized scores directly.
* We use a 6ND proxy for pretraining FLOPS, and 6 * max_tokens_per_rollout / max_context_length * n_rollouts * active_params proxy for RL FLOPS; that said, we are the only lab, as of this writing, which releases RL FLOPS, so meaningful comparisons are impossible. From the few labs who release midtraining / SFT information, we derive an unweighted mean percentage of FLOPS devoted to midtraining. We then estimate midtraining FLOPS for other labs using that mean. We estimate total FLOPS as the sum of pretraining FLOPS + (all midtraining / non-RL) FLOPS + (all RL and OPD) FLOPS. For any model which doesn't give sufficient evidence for any of the three stages, use the mean FLOPS over all models in the cohort as the estimated  FLOPS for that stage.
* In a separate standalone table, include all raw scores in XX.y format, with 95% confidence intervals derived from the trial count and the infrastructure error tolerance -- do not leave gaps, use table captions for results that require further context, use the exact same model family in the table as was present in the x-y scatterplot(s)
* Eval results are reportable IFF the eval in question completed with no more than 10% of trials encountering infrastructure errors
* Eval results are reportable IFF they include provenance, in the form of model traces, and where available, verifier traces
* Any eval result that is publicly presented should clearly distinguish whether the benchmarks are in-distribution (part of the dev set), held out, or a mix of the two
* Any eval result that is publicly presented in a major release should report on *all* ID and OOD benchmarks, avoiding cherry picking, substitution, or new evals outside of a formal policy update
* For active development and internal communication, it is fine to define working subsets of the ID benchmarks and report on those in isolation

## Future considerations

* We would like to post-train multiple Snowball checkpoints, experimenting with different degrees of compute applied to post-training, to establish trade-off lines / domains
* We would like to think about a "marin model card" that would set minimum standards for true open development
* amd/Instella-MoE-16B-A3B-Think is not runnable currently from our pinned vLLM fork, but we would like to look at this model in the future
* We still weren't able to land a trusted K2 Horizon baseline set of scores yet
* evaluate our baselines on OOD as well as ID
* JudgeArena multilingual, maybe one of those cultural idiom / include benchmarks, restore simpleQA-mini, a long context supplement for MRCR
* Produce a summary of why we think the previously flagged TB2 / TB4 task description overlap are likely not problematic, if they are not
* Use stirrup for at least one eval
* Find a better instruction following benchmark than IFBench
* Consider a subset of MMLU-Pro and tau-bench so they run faster

publicSources.body:
Agent-driven experiment issue: the runs and this record were produced by a Claude agent, supervised by @mcwitt.

## TL;DR

On one GB200 NVL72 rack, restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint at a fixed 4.19M tokens per step, 8K context trains at 297.0k tokens/s, 1.6% below 4K, and 16K at 292.5k tokens/s, 3.1% below 4K. The fraction of expert assignments dropped rises from 1.9e-4 at 4K to 8.3e-4 at 8K (4.5×) and 2.9e-3 at 16K (16×). All drops are on the sender side. Each arm has three seeds; the seed-to-seed standard deviation is at most 0.03 MFU points and 4% to 7% of the drop fraction.

## Description

The hero plan in #8435 moves from 4K to 8K sequences at 50% of training (step ~195k) and to 65K at ~95%. These runs measure what the 8K switch costs in throughput and expert-capacity drops before it happens, with 16K as the next point and a 4K control from the same checkpoint.

Setup:

* Source: `main` at f38da1173de79f1eacd5f54bcfb88db6cb0a9f6e with no code changes. Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_diagnostics.py`.

* Every arm keeps 4,194,304 tokens per step (65,536 per GPU), so the learning rate from the hero's heuristic (`MoeHeuristic` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/heuristic.py`, which scales with tokens per step and total tokens) is the same in all arms. `--schedule-steps 390251` is the hero's full schedule length, so the restored step sits at the hero's position in the learning-rate schedule.

* The trainer seed sets the data shuffle, so seeds 0, 1, and 2 train on different batches.
* Statistics cover steps 180010 to 180099 (90 steps). Each run contributes its median MFU, median tokens/s, and mean drop fraction; the tables report mean ± standard deviation across the three seeds. Starting the window at step 180030 instead moves no run's median MFU by more than 0.03 points.

| Arm | `--seq-len` | `--batch-size` | `--qk-mult` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K control | 4096 | 1024 | 1.3 |
| 8K | 8192 | 512 | 1.39 |


## Results

| Arm | tokens/s | vs 4K | step time | MFU | drop fraction | vs 4K |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K | 301.9k ± 0.2k | | 13.89 s | 28.25 ± 0.02% | 1.86e-4 ± 0.08e-4 | 1× |
| 8K | 297.0k ± 0.2k | −1.6% | 14.12 s | 28.47 ± 0.02% | 8.29e-4 ± 0.39e-4 | 4.5× |
| 16K | 292.5k ± 0.3k | −3.1% | 14.34 s | 29.37 ± 0.03% | 2.94e-3 ± 0.20e-3 | 16× |

Receiver-side drops were zero in every step of every run. Peak HBM was 103.1 GiB per GPU in every run. In every run, including the 4K control, the mean drop fraction over steps 180055 to 180099 was 0.75 to 1.00 times the mean over steps 180010 to 180054, so part of the measured drop fraction may be a transient after restore.

The live hero (11 racks, 4K) measured over steps 183310 to 183710 on 2026-09-30 had a median MFU of 26.47% and a mean drop fraction of 9.1e-5.

Caveats:

* MFU uses the analytic FLOP count, which charges more attention FLOPs per token at longer sequences (full causal attention on every fourth layer, a 2048-token window elsewhere). MFU therefore rises with sequence length while tokens/s falls. Compare arms by tokens/s.
* The one-rack 4K drop fraction is about 2× the 11-rack hero's. We have not tested the cause. The ratios between arms are the quantity to carry to the hero; an 8K hero drop fraction near 4e-4 is an extrapolation from that ratio, not a measurement.
* Each run covers 100 steps after the switch. Routing over thousands of steps at the new length is untested.
* The 8K and 16K arms change `qk_mult` together with sequence length.
* The diagnostic's peak learning rate comes from a one-rack token budget and is 0.69× the hero's. The diagnostic also leaves the attn_gate/router weight decay at 0 (the hero uses 0.02). Loss values are not comparable with the hero's.
* At 8K and 16K, XLA logged at compile time that rematerialization could only reduce its memory estimate to 193 GiB against a 161 GiB limit. The warning does not stop compilation. The runs trained normally with a runtime peak HBM of 103.1 GiB, the same as 4K, so the estimate overstated actual use.

* Hero plan: #8435. 262K context-parallel probe on the same hardware: #8754.

## Conclusion

At the planned 4K to 8K switch, expect about 1.6% fewer tokens per second and about 4.5× the 4K drop fraction, still below 0.1% of assignments on one rack. At 16K the costs are 3.1% and 16×.

publicSources.title: [datakit] Register the hero quality data as Datakit steps
publicSources.body:
Register the hero quality data as two Datakit steps and make the store-ready
dataset a StepSpec output. `bucket.quality_step` reads three co-partitioned leaves
of a source (the normalized shard for row order, the fusion score leaf, and the
content-type leaf), applies the per-type calibration, and writes one shard per
basename with `source`, `id`, `content_type`, `raw_score`, `score` and
`quality_bucket` in the normalized row order. Its artifact is the `QualityScores`
the store already consumes, so `build_clustered_store` reads it unchanged.
`hero_data.quality` resolves that step's identity, and `run.py --stage bucket`
produces it for every registered source.

`score_fusion.fusion_score_step` is the producer of record for the raw scores: one
Zephyr task per normalized shard on GPU workers, tokenizing the text through the
tokenize stage's own core and reading the Harrier embedding by position. The Nemotron
tokenize leaves the August 14 run read were deleted from S3 after it, so the run's
scores are registered by path map as `hero_data.fusion_scores` rather than
rescored; a rerun of the score stage lands at the step's own identity. The
content-type leaves written beside those scores are registered the same way as
`hero_data.content_type`, and `hero_data.harrier` now returns a frozen step so the
score step can depend on it.

Every input leaf of a source holds the normalized shard's documents in its row
order. A census over all 162,535 shards of the 292 sources found every
fusion-score, content-type and Harrier shard in exactly the normalized order, with
the same ids and row counts. Both steps therefore read their side inputs by
position and check each batch's ids against the normalized shard, so a leaf from a
different normalize run fails its shard. `QualityScores.samples_output_dir` is
removed; the stage report reads its spot-check text from the normalized shard of
the same basename.

The model directory moves to `datakit/models/quality/nemotron_88k`, relative to
`MARIN_PREFIX`, with the config fields of the removed bigram, MoE, frozen-donor
and dtype arms dropped from `model.py` and the saved meta. `QualityPin` carries
separate digests for the scorer artifacts and the calibration file, checked by the
worker before it writes, so a refit calibration moves the bucketed dataset without
moving or rescoring the raw scores. Manifest entries for `harrier`, `fusion_scores`,
`content_type` and `quality` cover all 292 sources. The fusion checkpoint's
document-embedding weights form one optional `DocFusion` submodule whose field
order matches the serialized leaves, so the deployed checkpoint loads to identical
weights and scores, and the calibration file parses into a `Calibration`
dataclass.

The bucket stage has run over all 292 sources: 18,710,478,349 documents in
162,535 shards, equal to the fusion-score totals, in 2h50m with 12 sources in
flight on CPU workers. On `nsf_awards` (3 shards, 381,789 documents) the output
reproduced the normalized row order, the pinned raw scores and content types, and
the calibrated buckets on every row. The score stage run from text against the
same embeddings matched the pinned scores to a maximum difference of 1.6e-3 (mean
2.3e-4), the bf16 reduction-order noise of a 4,096-document batch against the
earlier 32,768.

publicSources.title: [grug] Register symmetric buffers for hero all-gather and reduce-scatter
publicSources.body:
On the ragged all-to-all backend, the hero template registers NCCL symmetric buffers for the model's all-gather and reduce-scatter collectives in addition to the ragged transport. Levanter's `RAGGED_REQUIRED_XLA_FLAGS` keeps only the `raggedalltoall` registration that the device-initiated transport needs, so other users of that constant, such as the ragged EP test harness, are unchanged. The template keeps the flag non-overridable, like the transport flags.

Against #9333 alone, this change makes a typical update 0.24% faster, but it does not yet show a significant gain in mean throughput. Each arm ran twice on the same rack of 64 GB200 GPUs, in the order #9333, this PR, this PR, #9333. The trees were #9333 at `f56f7e6a9e` and this PR at `2698045acf`, which differ only in this change. The #9333 tree has the same dependency locks, hero model, training, and kernel code as `main` after #9333 merged. Each run restored the permanent hero `2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-30000` checkpoint with the production data mixture, batch 1024, sequence length 4096, and one process per GPU. Each run discarded 20 warmup updates and scored the 40 updates from 30020 through 30059. Every run sees the same batch at each step, so steps are compared across arms by step number.

| Configuration | Mean step time | Median step time | Mean iteration time | MFU | Runs |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| #9333 | 13.917 s | 13.906 s | 14.146 s | 28.21% | [a](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-symab2-base-a-20260923), [b](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-symab2-base-b-20260923) |
| This PR | 13.905 s | 13.882 s | 14.128 s | 28.23% | [a](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-symab2-sym-a-20260923), [b](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-symab2-sym-b-20260923) |

This PR was faster on 34 of 40 matched steps (sign test p = 8e-6). Two updates in run a took 14.96 s and 14.40 s. Excluding those steps, it saves 33 ms per update (standard error 6 ms), or 0.24%. Including them, mean training throughput improves by 0.09% (95% bootstrap interval −0.17% to +0.27%), and iteration throughput by 0.13%. None of the #9333 runs had an update slower than 14.18 s. In an earlier campaign on the same rack, updates slower than 14.3 s occurred in all three arms, including the #9366 control, so these runs do not show whether symmetric buffers cause them. Losses stayed finite. The largest matched-step loss difference was 0.00051, the same as between the two #9333 runs. An earlier three-run campaign, on the same rack and an earlier revision of #9333, measured a 0.32% mean gain ([a](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-maskab-both-a-20260922), [b](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-maskab-both-b-20260922), [c](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-maskab-both-c-20260922)).

Without the mask removal, symmetric buffers had no mean benefit: on PR #9228 revision `b688829e3d`, they measured −0.03% against the control ([a](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-opt-fa4-symmetric-a-20260922), [b](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-opt-fa4-symmetric-b-20260922), [c](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-opt-fa4-symmetric-c-20260922)), and slow updates in two repetitions erased an improvement in the median. A full [d768 run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-opt-d768-replayed-treatment-20260922) of 11,420 updates with both changes completed 20 dropless evaluations and matched the [historical control](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/validate9215-d768-20260917) to +0.000105 nats mean training loss.

Two risks remain untested at hero scale. The hero's parameters shard only within a rack, so each all-gather and reduce-scatter buffer should be the same size at 1 and 11 racks; whether XLA lowers any cross-rack gradient reduction as a symmetric-registered reduce-scatter or all-gather has not been checked. The dropless evaluator now also registers a symmetric window. #8861 showed that XLA resolves an address to the last window registered at the collective-memory arena base, so a smaller eval window can shadow the train step's; the d768 run passed its evaluations, but the hero shape has not been tested with interleaved evaluation.

Draft until those checks run.

publicSources.title: [grug] Hide the ragged MoE transports under compute
publicSources.body:
Raise the hero step's communication/compute overlap from 60% to 81% of collective time on one rack. The ragged backend now pipelines its two expert chunks, and the model keeps small collectives out of the transports' windows. A profile-guided latency estimate lets XLA place each transport under enough compute.

The hero runs with collective overlap limited to 1, so a single collective can be in flight. Before this change, the ragged transport serialized its chunks behind a barrier, so the first dispatch and first return had no GEMM to hide under. Small collectives also took the only slot inside the MoE section: the transpose rule's two offset all-to-alls, the FSDP gathers of the latent and shared-expert weights, and the router's QB pmin/pmax/histogram reductions. XLA also rematerialized the attention weight gathers after scheduling as exposed synchronous all-gathers. Each commit removes one of these causes:

- The chunks run as a two-stage pipeline, so chunk 1's dispatch overlaps chunk 0's expert MLP and chunk 0's return overlaps chunk 1's.
- The backward takes its transfer offsets from the mirror parameters instead of exchanging them. A test checks that the two parameter sets are each other's transpose.
- The attention projections re-gather their weights for the backward at the JAX level, as ordinary async all-gathers.
- The MLP-section weights are gathered before routing, and the QB statistics run after the routed MLP. A forward-only barrier enforces both, so the gradient reduce-scatters still fuse.

The code changes alone leave overlap near 60% and slow the step by 1.3%. XLA's default estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so it hides a 3-5 ms ragged transport under one GEMM. The last commit adds `pgle_profile.py`, which turns one XProf trace into a latency profile for `--xla_gpu_pgle_profile_file_or_directory_path`. The README documents the trace, build, and rerun workflow. The profile matches instructions by name, so it is rebuilt for each program and is not committed.

Measured on one GB200 rack restored from the hero's `step-144000`, batch 1024, with production XLA flags. Overlap is kernel-classified, as in the [baseline comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5821773936):

| | overlap | exposed collective | step |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| main (2026-09-24 baseline) | 60.5% | 1.51 s | 13.94 s |
| this branch | 60.2% | 1.55 s | 14.13 s |
| this branch + its PGLE profile | 81.0% | 0.88 s | 13.72 s |

The last row is W&B run `overlap80-v2-pgle-144k`. Its step time is 1.6% shorter than the baseline's. Loss matches the baseline to within 3e-4 at every step. Overlap is measured on one rank and depends on which: the same program and profile measure 72.5% on rank 37, whose GPU runs the step's compute 5% faster than rank 0's and spends the difference waiting inside collectives ([details](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5860234620)). Collective busy time rises from 3.8 to 4.6 s, because a transport overlapped with a GEMM runs slower. The trace covers only rack-local collectives, and the 11-rack production program would need its own profile. The production recipe still runs without PGLE, so deploying these commits alone would slow the hero rather than speed it up.

publicSources.title: [datakit] Add the content-type step and chain the quality pipeline
publicSources.body:
Add `content_type.content_type_step`, which predicts each document's content type
from its Harrier embedding with the `domain_mlp_v1` classifier: one Zephyr task
per normalized shard on CPU workers, writing `id`, `content_type`,
`content_type_prob` and the full 7-way `content_type_probs` in the normalized row
order. It replaces `type_corpus.py`, the script that wrote the August content
types and never landed. The full distribution is kept because the classifier
under-recalls the residual `other` class, and correcting that is a per-class
logit shift that needs every class's probability. The classifier is pinned as
`hero_data.DOMAIN_MLP_V1` by the sha256 of its weight file and its label order,
and the step refuses other bytes or a head with other labels.

`run.py --stage pipeline` chains the three quality steps: fusion scores, content
types, then buckets, each fed by the one before and landing at its own identity.
`run.py --stage bucket` still rebuckets the inputs `hero_data` pins, at the path
`hero_data.quality` resolves. Nothing registered in `hero_data` moves: the pinned
content-type and fusion-score maps change only when a fresh run is deliberately
registered in their place, and the manifest test holds every hero path fixed.

The three quality steps share one per-shard driver,
`shards.map_normalized_shards`: it pairs the normalized shards with their side
leaves by basename, runs one Zephyr task per shard, and writes under the same
basename, with `ShardPool` carrying the worker, task and max-worker sizing. The
co-partition helpers move beside it from `score_fusion`. On a 2,000-document slice
run locally with the real fusion checkpoint, tokenizer and classifier, the fusion
score and bucket steps write bit-identical output before and after the move.

On `common-crawl-focus-2026-22` shard 0 (66,106 documents) the step reproduces
the August content types on every document and their probabilities to within
2.1e-6.

publicSources.body:

publicSources.title: [levanter] Prefetch W&B metric transfers before converting them
publicSources.body:
W&B payload conversion now starts the device-to-host copy for every `jax.Array` leaf before reading any of them. It previously read each scalar with its own blocking copy. On the 535B-A23B Hero run that cost was most of the host time between optimizer steps: about 0.19 s per update for 780 router values, and 0.77 s on the watch updates every 10 steps, which log 3,572 values ([attribution](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9205#issuecomment-5901019798)).

On one GB200, with Hero-shaped payloads produced by a jitted function, converting 828 router-metric leaves took 175 ms before and 58 ms after (median of 120 trials). Converting 3,592 leaves including watch stats took 740 ms before and 269 ms after. A plain `jax.device_get` of the same payloads took 53 ms and 255 ms, so about 70 µs per leaf remains. Packing per-layer metrics into fewer arrays would remove most of that.

Non-primary hosts still materialize payloads while suppressing W&B output, as #5415 requires. The comment that described suppressed trackers as no-ops is corrected.

publicSources.title: [datakit] Tokenize ahead of the quality model and vectorize the remap
publicSources.body:
Tokenize up to two batches ahead of the pooled quality model on worker threads
while the model scores the current batch, and replace the per-token Python dict
remap with a numpy lookup table. `PooledScorer` now exposes the two halves,
`encode` (begin/middle/end windows, tokenizer, remap) and `predict_ids`;
`score_normalized` runs them on different threads inside each shard. Output
files keep their per-file order and naming, so the store's positional join is
unaffected. One encode at scorer load converts the 250K-vocab tokenizer and
fixes its truncation state before the prefetch threads share it.

Measured on the same 34,998 normalized documents with the kimi-labeled scorer,
one worker, outputs identical before and after in every run:

| hardware | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CPU (JAX CPU, warm process) | 30 to 32 s | 21 to 22 s |
| A100-SXM4-40GB (JAX CUDA) | 33.1 to 34.2 s | 28.4 to 30.7 s |

Per 512-document batch on the A100 the forward pass takes 7 ms and
tokenization 240 ms, so the GPU sits idle and the stage is bound by Python-side
tokenizer work; the remaining gap on the GPU is the tokenizer's Python-level
output conversion holding the GIL, which the threads cannot overlap. Returning
numpy arrays from the tokenizer instead of Python lists is the next step for
the accelerator case and is left out of this change.
